title: A single word in a question can change what you remember seeing
body: In a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people watched film of a car crash and were asked how fast the cars were going when they ‘smashed into’ or ‘hit’ each other. The word ‘smashed’ led to higher speed estimates, and a week later those people were more likely to recall broken glass that was never in the film. Memory isn’t a recording; each recall is a reconstruction that later information can quietly reshape.

slides.question: After a film of a car crash, how fast did people say the cars went when they ‘smashed into’ each other?
slides.explanation: About 41 mph, against about 34 mph when the question said ‘hit’, for the very same film.

slides.heading: Average speed estimate for the same crash film
slides.note: Loftus and Palmer, 1974. A week on, the ‘smashed’ group more often recalled broken glass.

slides.heading: Same film, new memories
slides.text: Changing just the verb shifted average speed estimates for the very same film, from about 34 mph for ‘hit’ to about 41 mph for ‘smashed’.

slides.heading: Whole events can be planted
slides.text: Later studies showed that suggestion can lead some people to ‘remember’ entire events that never happened, such as getting lost in a shopping mall as a child.

slides.heading: Why it matters
slides.text: Eyewitness memories can feel vivid and certain yet still be distorted by leading questions, which is why careful, neutral interviewing matters.

slides.heading: Fact or myth?

items.text: Memory works like a video recording
One word in a question can change what people recall
People can be led to ‘remember’ events that never happened
A vivid, confident memory is always an accurate one

slides.explanation: Each recall is a reconstruction, which is why leading questions can quietly reshape what a witness remembers.
